newsitem.title: UK: Mark options good value for hedging EMU turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Mark options good value for hedging EMU turmoil.

text.p: Concerns over an upset to Europe's monetary union timetable may have eased ahead of next week's EU summit meeting, but currency options dealers say opportunities remain in betting on further EMU turmoil.

As the mark has edged lower against its European satellites, currency option volatilities have also been marked down, but dealers say these lower levels offer a cheap opportunity to hedge against EMU risk.

"Vols offer good value at these levels," said Ian Groome, of ABN-Amro's options marketing team in London. "People are expecting a fudged EMU agreement so spot's come off and vols are lower. But you can buy cheap protection here in case the EMU process breaks down next week."
One-month mark/French franc volatility was trading at 2.0/2.3 percent against 2.1/2.6 percent late Thursday and this week's peak of 2.5/3.0 percent.
Mark/lira one-month volatility was trading at 4.7/5.2 percent, down from a peak this week of 5.75/6.25 percent.

Mark cross option risk reversals, the difference in implied volatility of calls relative to puts, continue to be skewed towards mark calls, implying ongoing demand for protection against mark strength.

"Mark crosses are very sensitive to spot moves at the moment," said Sara Sullivan, senior manager of global FX option sales at HSBC Midland. "If EMU goes ahead as planned, then vols will come down. But if there is any sign of delay, the mark will strengthen and vols will go higher."
For some time, dealers have been buying deep out-of-the-money mark calls against other European currencies as a cheap hedge or bet on a delay to EMU.
These trades offer the best risk to reward ratio, said traders, costing relatively little for potentially huge rewards, particularly in mark/lira.
"The only reason (spot) mark/lira's come down from the 1100-1200 levels is purely because of EMU," said a U.S. bank dealer. "So there is huge upside potential if EMU disappears."

"An EMU delay would affect all the crosses but the difference is if mark/lira kicks off, vols would probably go from five to 15 percent, where in mark/Paris you'll see a move from maybe 2.5 to six percent."
Mark/lira's relatively higher volatility level than its neighbouring EMU hopefuls reflects the market's perception that Italy is the least likely to qualify for EMU in 1999.

But the lira's volatility levels are also attributed to the high mark/lira forward rate which, if Italy managed a first-wave EMU start at its ERM parity of 990 per mark, would see spot lira soar to adjust to this lower forward rate.
So far, the market is taking a wait-and-see attitude ahead of next week's Amsterdam summit, but dealers said this certainly will not be the last opportunity to capitalise on EMU uncertainty.
"After the summer when Europe comes back from their holidays, we'll probably see another round of EMU crisis in the autumn, so vols are good value out there too," said ABN Amro's Groome.
